metaData.originalTitle: The last six months in LLMs in five minutes
metaData.title: The last six months in LLMs in five minutes
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Simon Willison's PyCon US 2026 lightning talk summarizes the last six months of LLM developments, highlighting the November 2025 inflection point where coding agents became reliably useful and local models began to wildly outperform expectations.
metaData.summary: In this annotated lightning talk from PyCon US 2026, Simon Willison covers the key LLM developments from November 2025 to May 2026. He identifies November 2025 as a critical inflection point, particularly for coding. The 'best' model title changed hands five times among Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. The real breakthrough was that coding agents, powered by Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards, crossed a quality barrier from 'often-work' to 'mostly-work,' becoming reliable daily drivers. The talk also covers the rise of 'Claws' (personal AI assistants), exemplified by the OpenClaw project, which started as an obscure repo in November and took the world by storm by February. Other highlights include Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro producing remarkably good SVG illustrations, the release of capable open-weight models like Google's Gemma 4 and China's GLM-5.1 and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the latter of which ran on a laptop and outperformed a frontier model on a specific creative task. Willison concludes that the two main themes are the maturation of coding agents and the surprising performance of local, laptop-available models.

mainPoints.point: November 2025 marked a critical inflection point for LLMs, especially for coding agents.
mainPoints.explanation: Coding agents transitioned from 'often-work' to 'mostly-work,' crossing a quality barrier that made them reliable daily drivers for real work, thanks to Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards.

mainPoints.point: The 'best' model title changed hands five times between Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google.
mainPoints.explanation: The rapid succession of model releases (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3, GPT-5.1 Codex Max, Claude Opus 4.5) illustrates the intense competition and fast pace of frontier model development.

mainPoints.point: Personal AI assistants, or 'Claws,' emerged as a major new category, exemplified by OpenClaw.
mainPoints.explanation: The OpenClaw project, which started in November 2025, became a phenomenon by February 2026, with people buying Mac Minis to run their own 'Claws,' likened to digital pets in an aquarium.

mainPoints.point: Local, laptop-available models are starting to wildly outperform expectations.
mainPoints.explanation: Models like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (20.9GB) running on a laptop could outperform a frontier model like Claude Opus 4.7 on a specific creative task, highlighting the growing capability of open-weight models.

mainPoints.point: The 'pelican riding a bicycle' test has exceeded its limits as a useful benchmark.
mainPoints.explanation: As models become increasingly capable at generating creative SVGs, this once-useful test for comparing model capabilities is no longer a reliable differentiator.

keyQuotes: Coding agents went from often-work to mostly-work, crossing a quality barrier where you could use them as a daily-driver to get real work done, without needing to spend most of your time fixing their stupid mistakes.
The coding agents got really good... and the laptop-available models, while a lot weaker than the frontier, have started wildly outperforming expectations.
Mac Minis started to sell out around Silicon Valley, because people were buying them to run their Claws.
I think this mainly demonstrates that the pelican on the bicycle has firmly exceeded its limits as a useful benchmark.
My favourite metaphor for Claws is Alfred Molina's Doc Ock in the 2004 movie Spider-Man 2.
